Count all the ring corners plus the two short methyl branches, you should find 19 carbons and 2 oxygens in total.

walkthrough:
**Understand Skeletal Formula Rules**

Every vertex (corner) and every free end of a line represents a carbon atom. Hydrogen atoms are hidden, but each carbon must have four bonds in total.

Rule:
$$\text{number of H on C} = 4 - (\text{bonds shown to C and other atoms})$$

**Count Carbon and Oxygen Atoms**

Look at the four fused rings. The three 6-membered rings plus the one 5-membered ring give 17 ring carbons. Add the two methyl groups sticking up, one on the 6-membered ring and one on the 5-membered ring.

Count:
$$17 \text{ (ring C)} + 2 \text{ (methyl C)} = 19 \text{ C}$$ 
There is one $\text{C=O}$ and one $\text{C-OH}$, so there are 2 O atoms.

**Count Hidden Hydrogens**

Now fill in hydrogens to make four bonds per carbon. Most $\text{CH}_2$ groups in the rings have 2 H each. Adjust for special carbons: the $\text{C=O}$ carbon has 0 H, the two $\text{C=C}$ carbons have 0 H and 1 H (one carries the methyl), the two bridgehead carbons where rings join have 1 H each, and the $\text{C-OH}$ carbon has 1 H.

Careful total:
$$\text{H on carbons} + \text{H on OH} = 27 + 1 = 28$$

**Write the Molecular Formula**

Combine your counts for C, H and O.

$$\text{C}_{19}\text{H}_{28}\text{O}_{2}$$
This matches the known formula for testosterone.

options.A: Correct. There are 19 carbons (17 in the steroid ring system + 2 methyls), 2 oxygens, and 28 hydrogens when every carbon is given four bonds. This gives $\text{C}_{19}\text{H}_{28}\text{O}_{2}$.
options.B: Incorrect. $\text{C}_{17}$ counts only the ring carbons and misses the two methyl ($\text{CH}_3$) branches. In skeletal formulas, short lines sticking out are also carbons and must be included.
options.C: Incorrect. Like B, it misses the two methyl carbons to give only 17 C. The H count is also wrong because if you miss carbons you automatically miss their hydrogens too.
options.D: Incorrect. The carbon and oxygen counts are right, but H is two too low. This often happens if you count one extra double bond or forget that the $\text{OH}$ group contributes one H plus the $\text{C=C}$ changes H count by only two, not four.
